title: The General Who May Never Have Lived
author: Sun Tzu
wiifm: The most quoted book on strategy in the world is about thirteen short chapters long, and almost nothing about its author can be proved. That turns out to be a lesson in itself. The Art of War is not a manual of tactics. It is a way of thinking about contests: win before you fight, know yourself and the other side, never let a struggle drag on, and treat the enemy's mind as the real target. We follow the legend of a general called Sun Wu, clearly marked as legend, and then the true and stranger life of the book itself.

ch.h: A story told four hundred years later
b: Begin with an honest admission, because the book itself would approve of it. We do not know who Sun Tzu was. We are not even sure he existed. The name means Master Sun, a title of respect rather than a name, and the only real biography of him was written by the Han dynasty historian Sima Qian, who finished his great history around 90 BC. Sima Qian was describing a man who, if he lived at all, had been dead for roughly four centuries.

Sima Qian's account says that Sun Wu came from the state of Qi, on the eastern coast of what is now China, and offered his services to King Helü of Wu, a rising southern kingdom, around the year 512 BC. This was the age the Chinese call the Spring and Autumn period, when the old Zhou royal house had shrunk to a ceremony and dozens of states fought, married and betrayed one another in a slow tournament of survival.

The trouble is that the other big chronicle of that era, the Zuo Zhuan, which records the wars of Wu in some detail, never mentions Sun Wu at all. A general who supposedly helped Wu humble its giant neighbour Chu ought to have left a mark. He left none. So what follows is the legend, told as the Chinese have told it for two thousand years, and we will come back to the evidence when the story is done.
ch.cap: Sima Qian brushes Sun Wu's story onto bamboo

b: The story goes like this. King Helü had read Sun Wu's thirteen chapters and wanted a demonstration. Could the method be tried, he asked, on women? Sun Wu said it could. So one hundred and eighty women of the palace were brought out into the courtyard, and Sun Wu divided them into two companies, with one of the king's two favourite concubines in command of each.

He explained the drill carefully. Front meant look ahead, left meant turn to the left hand, right meant the right, back meant turn around. He repeated the instructions several times. Then the drums sounded the order to face right, and the women burst out laughing.

Sun Wu said that if orders are unclear, the fault lies with the general. He explained again. The drums sounded the order to face left. The women laughed again. This time, he said, the orders had been clear, so the fault lay with the officers, and he ordered both captains beheaded. The king, watching from a terrace, sent a frantic message that he was satisfied and could not bear to lose the two women. Sun Wu replied that a general in command of the army need not accept every order of his sovereign, and had them executed. He appointed the next two women as captains, sounded the drums, and the whole company wheeled, knelt and stood in perfect silence.

It is a brutal story and almost certainly a moral fable rather than a report. But notice what it is teaching, because the whole book is folded inside it. First make yourself clearly understood, and take the blame if you have not. Then hold people to what was clear. And once the commander is in the field, the person back at the palace should not be running the battle.
ch.cap: Palace women laugh at the drum; Sun Wu waits

ch.h: War is a matter of life and death
b: The book opens not with fighting but with a warning. War, it says, is a matter of vital importance to the state, the ground of life and death, the road to survival or ruin. It must be examined with great care. That sentence sets the tone for everything after it. This is not a celebration of combat. It is a book written by someone who thought war was usually a disaster and wanted it handled like one.

So the first chapter is about calculation, done in a temple before any army moves. Sun Tzu lists five fundamentals to weigh. The first is the Way, meaning whether the people are united with their ruler so they will follow him through danger. Then heaven, meaning weather and seasons, and earth, meaning distance, terrain and safety. Then the commander, judged on wisdom, sincerity, humanity, courage and strictness. Finally method and discipline, which is organisation, supply and the chain of command.

Compare both sides honestly on all five, and you can predict the result before a single soldier marches. The side that calculates more wins, the book says, and the side that calculates less loses, and the side that does not calculate at all has no chance.

This is the first great idea, and it is the one most people skip past on the way to the clever bits. Victory is mostly decided before the contest. A good strategist does the sums first and only fights when the sums say yes.
ch.cap: Before marching, counting rods weigh the five fundamentals

ch.h: All warfare is based on deception
b: Then comes the line everyone knows. All warfare is based on deception. When able to attack, seem unable. When near, make the enemy believe you are far away. Offer bait to lure him. Feign disorder and then strike. If he is angry, irritate him further. If he is rested, wear him out. Attack where he is unprepared and appear where you are not expected.

It is easy to read this as a manual for trickery. It is really an argument about information. The enemy commander is making decisions based on what he believes. Change what he believes and you change what he does, often at very little cost to you. The real battlefield, in other words, is in the other general's head.

Alongside this the book introduces a pair of ideas that run through Chinese strategy ever since: zheng and qi, usually translated as the orthodox and the unorthodox. The orthodox force engages the enemy in the way he expects. The unorthodox force then wins by doing what he does not expect. Sun Tzu says the two are endlessly combined, like the five musical notes producing more melodies than anyone can hear, and that each can turn into the other.

He also uses the word shi, which translators render as energy, momentum or strategic advantage. His images are memorable. Shi is like a torrent of water rolling boulders along, or like a round stone rolled down a mountain thousands of feet high. A skilled general does not demand too much of individual soldiers. He arranges the situation so that the situation does the work.
ch.cap: Banners hold the ridge while a hidden column slips round

b: The third chapter contains what many readers think is the heart of the whole book. To fight and conquer in all your battles is not the supreme excellence. Supreme excellence is breaking the enemy's resistance without fighting at all.

Sun Tzu then gives a ranking. The best thing is to attack the enemy's strategy, so his plan fails before it begins. Next best is to disrupt his alliances, so he stands alone. Next is to attack his army in the field. The worst of all is to besiege walled cities, which takes months of preparation and costs the lives of a third of your men, and still may fail.

Hand in hand with this goes a hatred of long wars. There has never been a country, the book says, that benefited from prolonged warfare. An army far from home drains the treasury, raises prices, exhausts the farmers who supply it, and invites neighbouring states to take advantage. Speed matters more than polish. A quick, clumsy victory beats a slow, clever one.

Sun Tzu then lists five ways of knowing who will win. The side wins that knows when to fight and when not to; that knows how to handle both large and small forces; whose ranks are united in purpose; that is prepared and waits to take the enemy unprepared; and whose general is capable and not interfered with by the sovereign. That last point echoes the courtyard story. A ruler who meddles from a distance in matters he cannot see, the book warns, merely hobbles his army.

And then the most famous sentence of all. If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles. If you know yourself but not the enemy, for every victory you will suffer a defeat. If you know neither, you will lose every time. The usual quotation says you will win a hundred battles, but the original is more careful. It says you will not be in danger. Knowledge does not guarantee triumph. It guarantees you will not be destroyed by surprise.
ch.cap: Two armies stand still; an envoy carries terms between

b: In the legend, Sun Wu's thinking was then tested for real. Sima Qian says that under his command Wu defeated the great state of Chu in the west, and entered its capital, Ying. That campaign is historical. Wu did take Ying in 506 BC after a series of victories, and the Zuo Zhuan credits it to King Helü, his brother and a brilliant exile from Chu named Wu Zixu. Whether Sun Wu was there is exactly what we cannot confirm.

Whoever won it, the book describes how such victories are made. A good general first makes himself invincible, then waits for the enemy to become vulnerable. Invincibility depends on you. Vulnerability depends on the enemy. So the victorious army wins first and then seeks battle, while the defeated army fights first and then hopes to win.

The fullest image comes in chapter six, on strength and weakness. An army should be like water. Water flows away from high places and fills the low ones. An army should avoid the enemy's strength and strike his weakness. Water has no constant shape, and in war there are no constant conditions. The one who can change with his opponent and still win may be called divine.

This is why The Art of War offers so few rules and so many principles. It deliberately refuses to give you a formula, because a formula is something the enemy can learn. What it gives you is a habit of reading the ground, the weather and the other side, and shaping yourself to fit.
ch.cap: Wu's boats flow round the rocks toward Ying

b: The final chapter of the book is about spies, and it is one of the most modern things written in the ancient world. Sun Tzu points out the arithmetic. Raising an army of a hundred thousand men costs a fortune every day and keeps seven hundred thousand households from their work. To fight for years over a single day's victory, and then begrudge a hundred ounces of silver for information, is the height of inhumanity.

Foreknowledge, he insists, cannot be had from spirits, from comparing past events, or from calculations of the stars. It must come from people who know the enemy's situation. He lists five kinds of spy: local spies drawn from the enemy's population, inside spies among his officials, double agents turned from his own spies, doomed spies fed false information so they will be caught and repeat it, and surviving spies who go and come back with reports.

Of these, the double agent matters most, because he leads you to all the others. And the book says the general must treat spies more intimately and reward them more generously than anyone else in the army.
It is a fitting place to end. The book that began with calculation in the temple finishes with the source of every good calculation: accurate knowledge, paid for properly and protected closely.
ch.cap: A cloaked spy hands over sealed news for silver

ch.h: The real life of the book
b: Now step out of the legend. Most scholars think The Art of War took shape in the Warring States period, roughly the fifth to the fourth century BC, a little after Sun Wu's supposed lifetime. The book describes huge conscript armies, professional generals and long campaigns that fit that later era better than the smaller aristocratic wars around 500 BC. It may be the work of a school of thinkers, gathered under a famous name, and edited over generations.

In 1972, archaeologists excavating Han dynasty tombs at Yinqueshan, in Shandong province, found bundles of bamboo slips buried around the second century BC. Among them was a version of the Sun Tzu text, close to the one we know, and a long-lost companion work by Sun Bin, said to be a descendant of Sun Wu, who fought in the fourth century. The find proved the book was old and widely read in the early Han, though it did not settle who wrote it.

The thirteen-chapter text we read today owes a great deal to Cao Cao, the warlord of the late Han, who wrote the earliest surviving commentary around 200 AD. In 1772 a French Jesuit in Beijing, Jean Joseph Marie Amiot, produced the first European translation. The best known English version, by Lionel Giles of the British Museum, appeared in 1910. In the twentieth century Mao Zedong drew on it in his guerrilla writings, and from the 1980s onwards it became a favourite of business schools and boardrooms.
ch.cap: Archaeologists lift bamboo slips from a Han tomb, 1972

b: The tale of Wu itself ends with a twist the book would have understood. King Helü died in 496 BC of a wound received fighting the neighbouring state of Yue. His son Fuchai beat Yue, spared its king, and turned his attention north to win prestige. Yue's king waited, rebuilt, and in 473 BC destroyed Wu entirely. A state that had supposedly been taught to win without fighting, to avoid long wars and to know its enemy, was finished by an enemy it had underestimated and failed to finish.

So what do we actually have? Not a reliable biography. We have a set of ideas, tested by two and a half thousand years of readers, that hold up remarkably well. Calculate before you commit. Know yourself and the other side honestly. Win in the mind before you win on the ground. Prefer the bloodless victory. Keep contests short. Be shapeless enough that nobody can predict you. Pay properly for good information.

A word of caution belongs here too. Many popular quotations attributed to Sun Tzu online are not in the book at all, and translations vary a great deal. If you want to quote it, use a reputable translation and check the line.

Perhaps it is right that the general fades into legend. The book was never really about him. It was about a way of seeing a contest clearly, and that has outlived every state that once fought over it.
ch.cap: Wu's palace smoulders at dawn; the bamboo book survives

take: Sun Tzu's temple calculation compares both sides on five fundamentals before anyone marches. Before a big decision, write down honestly how you and your competitor compare, and only commit when the comparison favours you.

In the legend, the first failure was blamed on the general for unclear instructions. If your team gets something wrong, check first whether you explained it properly, and only then hold people to account.

The best victory breaks the other side's plan or alliances rather than meeting them head on. Look for ways to make a contest unnecessary, through positioning, partnerships or a better offer, before you compete on price.
No state ever benefited from prolonged war. Set time limits on projects and disputes, because the cost of dragging on grows quietly every week.
Make yourself hard to beat, then wait for the other side to expose a weakness. In business that means secure cash and capability before you chase growth.
Water takes the shape of the ground. Avoid competing where a rival is strongest, and flow toward the gaps they leave.
Sun Tzu thought it inhuman to spend fortunes on war and skimp on intelligence. Budget properly for knowing your customers, market and competitors.
Much of what circulates as Sun Tzu is invented. Use a good translation, and treat the ideas as principles to test rather than scripture.
recall: What do we actually know about Sun Tzu's life?

Very little. The only biography is by Sima Qian, written about four centuries later, and the main chronicle of the era never mentions him. Most scholars think the book was compiled in the Warring States period, perhaps by several hands.
What is the order of preference for attacking an enemy?
Best is to attack the enemy's strategy, next his alliances, then his army in the field. Worst of all is besieging walled cities, which is slow and costly.
What does the famous line about knowing the enemy actually say?

If you know the enemy and yourself, you need not fear a hundred battles. Know only yourself and you win some and lose some, know neither and you lose every time. The original promises safety from disaster, not guaranteed victory.
The orthodox and the unorthodox forces. The orthodox engages the enemy as expected, and the unorthodox wins by surprise, and the two endlessly combine and turn into each other.
What was found at Yinqueshan in 1972?
Han dynasty bamboo slips containing an early version of The Art of War and the lost work of Sun Bin. They proved the text was old and widely read by the second century BC.
note: Sun Wu's biography and the concubine story come from Sima Qian's Shiji, written about 90 BC; the Zuo Zhuan does not mention him, and most scholars regard both man and story as at least partly legendary. Wu's capture of Ying in 506 BC, Helü's death in 496 BC and Wu's destruction by Yue in 473 BC are historical. The Yinqueshan slips were found in 1972; Cao Cao's commentary, Amiot's 1772 French translation and Giles's 1910 English translation are documented. Dating the text to the Warring States period is the mainstream scholarly view but remains debated.
words: A cunning plan or trick designed to outwit an opponent.
The Art of War treats the stratagem as cheaper than the battle: change what the other general believes and you change what he does.
The gradual wearing down of strength through sustained loss.
Sun Tzu loathed wars of attrition, warning that no country ever benefited from a prolonged war that drains treasury, farms and morale.
Widely told or quoted but of doubtful authenticity.
The concubine story is probably apocryphal, and so are many of the Sun Tzu quotations that circulate online.
A careful critical explanation or interpretation of a text.
The warlord Cao Cao wrote the earliest surviving exegesis of the book around 200 AD, and much of the text we read today passed through his hands.
Favourable; giving a good chance of success.
Sun Tzu's general makes himself invincible first, then waits for a propitious moment when the enemy exposes a weakness.
stories: The general who beheaded the king's favourites

The story goes that King Helü of Wu read Sun Wu's thirteen chapters and asked for a demonstration using his palace women. Sun Wu formed one hundred and eighty of them into two companies, each led by one of the king's two favourite concubines, and explained the drill. At the drum to face right, they laughed. Unclear orders, he said, are the general's fault, and he explained again. They laughed again. Now the orders were clear, so the fault was the officers', and he had both captains beheaded over the king's pleas. The next pair took command and the company moved in perfect silence. Probably a fable, but the lesson is sharp: be clear, then hold people to it.
The book that came out of a tomb

For centuries some scholars suspected The Art of War was a much later work dressed up in an ancient name. Then in 1972 archaeologists excavating Han dynasty tombs at Yinqueshan, in Shandong province, lifted out bundles of bamboo slips buried around the second century BC. Among them was a version of Sun Tzu close to the text we read today, and something nobody had read for centuries: a lost military treatise by Sun Bin, said to be Sun Wu's descendant. The muddy slips proved the book was old and widely read in the early Han. The twist is that they still could not tell us who wrote it. The book was proved real; the author stayed a legend.
The kingdom that forgot its own lesson

Wu was supposedly the state Sun Wu served, and it took the great rival city of Ying in 506 BC. Ten years later King Helü died of a wound received fighting the small neighbouring state of Yue. His son Fuchai beat Yue, but spared its king, Goujian, and turned north to chase prestige. The story goes that Goujian slept on brushwood and tasted bitter gall to keep his humiliation fresh while he rebuilt. In 473 BC Yue destroyed Wu completely. The kingdom linked to the world's most famous book on knowing your enemy and finishing contests quickly was ended by an enemy it underestimated and left half beaten.
biz: Do the temple sums before you scale spend

Sun Tzu compared both sides on five fundamentals before any army moved. Do the same before raising budget on any channel. This week, score HomeownersLoan against two named competitors on five things you can actually check: lender panel breadth, speed to first contact, clarity of the landing page and its risk warning, review standing, and cost per completed case rather than cost per lead. Only push budget where the comparison favours you, and suggest that to whoever runs the ad accounts with the numbers attached. Measure cost per completed case by channel every month, because a cheap lead that never completes is a defeat that looks like a victory.
Pay properly for intelligence, and keep deception for rivals only

The spy chapter says it is folly to spend fortunes on war and skimp on information. Your cheapest intelligence is already in the building. Add a compulsory reason lost field to every closed enquiry in the CRM, listen to five recorded calls a week, and check rivals' live ads in the public Meta Ad Library monthly. One firm rule: Sun Tzu's deception is aimed at competitors' expectations, never at customers. Under Consumer Duty every claim to a homeowner or a debt client must be clear, fair and not misleading. Measure how many closed leads have a recorded reason and review the top three reasons each month.
connects: Both say do not attack a rival where he is strongest: Sun Tzu's water flows to the low ground, and Positioning tells you to find the empty slot in the customer's mind.
Sun Tzu's temple calculation, where the side that calculates more wins, is an ancient version of Tetlock's case for honest, numerical forecasting before you commit.
Boyd read Sun Tzu closely and turned the idea that the enemy's mind is the real target into the loop of observe, orient, decide and act.
recap:
Two and a half thousand years ago, in a China split into quarrelling states, a general called Sun Wu is said to have offered his services to King Helü of Wu. We say is said, because the only biography of him was written about four centuries later, and the main chronicle of his age never mentions him at all. The legend is vivid. Asked to drill the palace women, he had the king's two favourite concubines executed when the women laughed at his orders, and after that the company moved in perfect silence. First make yourself understood. Then hold people to it.

The book under his name is short, thirteen chapters, and it opens not with glory but with a warning. War is a matter of life and death for the state, and must be examined with great care. So the first big idea is calculation. Before any army marches, compare both sides honestly on the things that decide contests: unity, weather, ground, leadership and discipline. The side that does the sums wins before it fights.

The second idea is that the real battlefield is the other commander's mind. All warfare, the book says, is based on deception. Change what your opponent believes, and you change what he does, at little cost to yourself.

The third is that the best victory needs no battle at all. Attack the enemy's plan first, then his alliances, then his army, and only as a last resort his walled cities. And keep contests short, because no country ever benefited from a long war.

The fourth is the image of water. Water has no fixed shape. It avoids the high ground and fills the low places. An army should avoid strength, strike weakness, and change with its opponent, which is why the book offers principles rather than formulas that an enemy could learn.

The fifth is knowledge. Know the enemy and know yourself, and you need not fear a hundred battles. The final chapter is about spies, and it calls it inhuman to spend fortunes on war while begrudging silver for information.

The kingdom of Wu did not follow its own lesson. It beat its neighbour Yue, spared its king, turned away to chase prestige, and was destroyed by Yue a generation later. In nineteen seventy-two archaeologists found the text on bamboo slips in an ancient tomb, proving the book was old, though never who wrote it. The general faded into legend. The way of seeing survived.

The line to remember: win first in the mind, and only then on the ground.
